words.definition: To grow steadily worse and more poisoned when a wound or feeling is left unresolved.
words.example: The unspoken grudge began to fester until the two brothers could no longer share a room.
words.mnemonic: A 'fest' of germs throwing a party in an untreated cut — the longer it goes, the nastier it gets.

words.definition: To eat away at metal or material gradually through chemical reaction.
words.example: Years of salt spray had corroded the iron railings until they crumbled at a touch.
words.mnemonic: 'Core' + 'rode' — rust rode straight into the metal's core.

words.definition: To dry something out completely by removing all of its moisture.
words.example: The desert air desiccated the fallen leaves until they crumbled into powder.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'desert' + 'sick' — the desert makes everything sick and bone-dry.

words.definition: To shrink and wrinkle up, especially from heat, cold, or lack of water.
words.example: Left on the vine too long, the grapes shriveled into hard little raisins.
words.mnemonic: 'Shrivel' = 'shrink' and 'wrinkle' smashed together.

words.definition: To make something weaker, thinner, or less intense.
words.example: Thick concrete walls attenuated the traffic noise to a faint hum.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'tenuis' (thin) — 'a-TENU-ate' turns something tenuous and thin.

words.definition: To move back or withdraw gradually from a former position.
words.example: As the tide receded, a wide stretch of wet sand appeared.
words.mnemonic: 'Re-' (back) + 'cede' (go) — go back, like a receding hairline.

words.definition: To flow back or decline, as the sea does when the tide falls.
words.example: As the evening wore on, the crowd's excitement slowly ebbed away.
words.mnemonic: Short and shrinking — the tide pulling back; the opposite of 'flow'.

words.definition: To become gradually narrower or smaller toward one end.
words.example: The candle tapered to a thin point at the top.
words.mnemonic: A 'taper' is a slender candle — narrow at the tip, thinning as it goes.

words.definition: To drain someone's strength or energy little by little.
words.example: The relentless heat sapped the hikers of every last bit of energy.
words.mnemonic: Sap is a tree's lifeblood — drain the sap and it wilts, just like you.

words.definition: To drain of energy or vitality, leaving one weak and listless.
words.example: The long, humid afternoon left the whole office enervated and unable to focus.
words.mnemonic: Looks like 'energize' but means the opposite — 'e-NERVE-ate' cuts your nerve and energy out.

words.definition: To seriously weaken the strength or health of a person or thing.
words.example: A bout of pneumonia debilitated him so badly he could barely climb the stairs.
words.mnemonic: Hides 'debil-' like Spanish 'débil' (weak) — it makes you feeble.

words.definition: To break down and rot into simpler substances through natural decay.
words.example: The fallen log slowly decomposed, feeding mushrooms and beetles for years.
words.mnemonic: 'De-' (undo) + 'compose' — to un-compose, falling apart into pieces.

words.definition: Close to death or on the verge of ceasing to exist.
words.example: The once-thriving factory town was now moribund, its shops boarded and streets empty.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'mori' (to die), as in 'mortal' — it's nearly gone.

words.definition: Worn out and weakened by old age, long use, or neglect.
words.example: The decrepit old car wheezed, rattled, and finally gave up in the driveway.
words.mnemonic: 'Decayed' + 'crippled' — creaky and falling apart with age.

words.definition: Fallen into ruin or disrepair, especially a building or structure.
words.example: They bought the dilapidated farmhouse for almost nothing and spent years repairing the sagging roof.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'lapis' (stone) — its very stones are falling apart.

words.definition: Abandoned and left in a run-down, neglected condition.
words.example: The derelict factory had broken windows and weeds pushing up through its floors.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'dare-a-lick' — even a stray dog wouldn't dare lick this filthy, abandoned building.

words.definition: To begin growing and developing from a seed.
words.example: The beans will germinate within a week if you keep the soil warm and damp.
words.mnemonic: A 'germ' of an idea starts to grow — germinate begins with 'germ,' the tiny start of life.

words.definition: To start growing, sending up fresh shoots from a seed or plant.
words.example: After the spring rains, tiny green shoots began to sprout across the muddy field.
words.mnemonic: Sprout sounds like 'spurt out' — the new plant spurts out of the ground.

words.definition: To produce flowers, or to develop fully and beautifully.
words.example: The cherry trees blossom every April, filling the park with clouds of pink petals.
words.mnemonic: 'Bloss' echoes 'bloom' — both burst open into flower.

words.definition: To care for something and help it grow, develop, or thrive.
words.example: She nurtured the orphaned kittens with warm milk and constant attention until they thrived.
words.mnemonic: Nurture shares roots with 'nurse' and 'nourish' — all about feeding and caring for something.

words.definition: To encourage the development of something; also, to raise another person's child.
words.example: The teacher fostered a love of reading by filling the classroom with exciting books.
words.mnemonic: Think of a 'foster home,' where caregivers help a child grow up safely.

words.definition: To spread widely, or to produce new plants and offspring.
words.example: Gardeners propagate strawberries by planting the runners that creep out from each parent plant.
words.mnemonic: Propagate starts like 'propaganda' — both push something to spread far and wide.

words.definition: To grow bigger or increase in size, volume, or intensity.
words.example: His ankle began to swell after he twisted it on the rocky trail.
words.mnemonic: Picture a sponge dropped in water — it swells until it's twice its size.

words.definition: To swell or stretch outward, usually from internal pressure.
words.example: Weeks of famine had left the child's belly painfully distended.
words.mnemonic: Dis-TEND, like 'ex-tend' — Latin 'distendere,' to stretch apart until it bulges.

words.definition: Fully filled or abundantly supplied with something.
words.example: The ancient library was replete with rare manuscripts and long-forgotten maps.
words.mnemonic: Re-PLETE — like 'complete' and 'deplete,' the '-plete' root means fill; here, filled to the brim.

words.definition: Highly fertile and capable of producing much offspring or vegetation.
words.example: The fecund delta soil yielded three harvests a year without any fertilizer.
words.mnemonic: Shares a Latin root with 'fetus' — bursting with the ability to bring forth new life.

words.definition: Producing a great number of works, offspring, or results.
words.example: The prolific author published over sixty novels in her lifetime.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'prol-' like 'proliferate' — both mean multiplying rapidly.

words.definition: Widespread and very common, often describing something unwelcome.
words.example: Rumors of layoffs were rife throughout the office after the merger was announced.
words.mnemonic: Rife sounds like 'ripe' — when gossip is ripe, it's suddenly everywhere.

words.definition: To rise or move forward suddenly with great force.
words.example: The crowd surged toward the stage the moment the band walked into view.
words.mnemonic: Surge is 'urge' with an S — a powerful urge pushes forward like a breaking wave.

words.definition: To fly or rise high into the air, or to increase rapidly.
words.example: The eagle soared above the canyon without flapping its wings once.
words.mnemonic: The double 'o' in soar looks like two wings spread wide, carrying a bird ever higher.

words.definition: To increase greatly in number or quantity, often by breeding or repeated addition.
words.example: Rabbits multiply so fast that two can become dozens within a single year.
words.mnemonic: multi- means 'many'; picture copies stacking up until there are many.

words.definition: To grow back or restore something that was lost, damaged, or worn out.
words.example: A starfish can regenerate an arm that a predator has torn off.
words.mnemonic: re- (again) + generate (create) — to create it all over again.

words.definition: To give new energy, strength, or life to something weak or run-down.
words.example: The council planted trees and opened cafés to revitalize the dying downtown.
words.mnemonic: re- + 'vital' — put the vitalness back into something.

words.definition: Rising again and becoming strong or active after a period of decline.
words.example: The resurgent team clawed back from last place to win the championship.
words.mnemonic: re- (again) + surge — a wave that swells up once more.

words.definition: To slowly return to good health after being sick or injured.
words.example: After surgery, she went to the coast to convalesce for a quiet month.
words.mnemonic: Latin valere (to be strong) — think 'convalescent home' where you grow strong again.

words.definition: To regain health, strength, or losses after illness, exhaustion, or a setback.
words.example: He took two weeks off to recuperate after the exhausting deadline crunch.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 're-cooper' — a cooper rebuilds a broken barrel back to whole.

words.definition: To bounce back or recover quickly after a fall, defeat, or blow.
words.example: Stock prices rebounded sharply the very day after the crash.
words.mnemonic: re- (again) + bound (leap) — leap back up like a ball off the floor.

words.definition: The ability to recover quickly from hardship, stress, or difficult conditions.
words.example: Her resilience let her rebuild a whole life after the fire took everything.
words.mnemonic: From Latin salire (to jump) — you spring back after being pushed down.

words.definition: Strong and able to survive difficult conditions, cold, or rough treatment.
words.example: Only hardy plants like cacti can survive the desert's brutal heat.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'hard' — tough enough to take a beating and keep going.

words.definition: Great physical or mental energy, strength, and liveliness.
words.example: At ninety, his vitality amazed everyone as he bounded up the hill.
words.mnemonic: From Latin vita (life) — being utterly full of life.

words.definition: A severe, widespread shortage of food that causes hunger and starvation.
words.example: When the crops failed two years running, famine swept through the region.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'famished' — both mean desperately, dangerously hungry.

words.definition: A deadly, fast-spreading disease that kills many people at once.
words.example: The medieval pestilence wiped out a third of Europe's population.
words.mnemonic: 'pest' + -ilence — a pest so vast it becomes a killing plague.

words.definition: The spreading of disease or emotion from one person to another by contact.
words.example: Fear moved through the crowd like a contagion, and soon everyone was fleeing.
words.mnemonic: con- (with) + tag (touch, Latin tangere) — caught by touching.

words.definition: Physical or mental weakness, especially caused by old age or illness.
words.example: Age brought infirmity, and he could no longer climb the stairs unaided.
words.mnemonic: in- (not) + firm — no longer firm or sturdy.

words.definition: Physically weak and delicate, easily broken or harmed.
words.example: The frail old woman needed help to lift even a teacup.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'fail' — a frail thing fails the moment pressure hits it.

words.definition: Extremely thin and bony, often from illness, hunger, or exhaustion.
words.example: After weeks lost in the mountains, his gaunt face frightened the rescue team.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'want' — someone who badly wants food goes hollow and gaunt.

words.definition: Looking worn out and unwell from stress, tiredness, or suffering.
words.example: Three sleepless nights with the newborn left her haggard by Friday morning.
words.mnemonic: A witch, or 'hag,' is drawn and worn — a hag looks haggard.

words.definition: Abnormally thin and weak, usually from starvation or serious illness.
words.example: The rescued dogs were so emaciated that their ribs pressed against the skin.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'e-MEAT-iated' — all the meat has wasted off the bones.

words.definition: A state of physical or mental weariness and lack of energy.
words.example: A heavy lassitude settled over the office during the sticky afternoon heat.
words.mnemonic: 'Lazy attitude' slurred together becomes lassitude — no drive to move.

words.definition: A state of sluggish inactivity, dullness, or suspended physical function.
words.example: The bear sank into a winter torpor, barely stirring for months.
words.mnemonic: Torpor rhymes with 'stupor' — both leave you numb, slowed, and motionless.

words.definition: A lack of energy, alertness, and enthusiasm; a drowsy indifference.
words.example: The flu wrapped him in such lethargy that lifting a spoon felt heavy.
words.mnemonic: 'Let-thy-energy' drain away — that draining leaves you in lethargy.

words.definition: A general feeling of illness, discomfort, or unease with no clear cause.
words.example: A vague malaise hung over the town after the factory shut its doors.
words.mnemonic: French 'mal' (bad) + 'aise' (ease) = bad-ease, a feeling that something's off.

words.definition: The gradual slide of a system toward disorder, randomness, or decay.
words.example: Left unmaintained, the garden surrendered to entropy and vanished under weeds.
words.mnemonic: 'En-trophy' — but the trophy is rusting; everything drifts toward chaos.

words.definition: The process of breaking apart, ending, or formally disbanding something.
words.example: The partners signed papers marking the dissolution of their fifteen-year company.
words.mnemonic: Picture a sugar cube in water losing shape — the whole thing coming undone.

words.definition: The complete dying out or permanent disappearance of a species or thing.
words.example: Relentless hunting drove the passenger pigeon to extinction within a few decades.
words.mnemonic: Like a candle 'extinguished' — the flame is snuffed out and never returns.

words.definition: Left unplanted or inactive for a time so it can rest and recover.
words.example: The farmer let the north field lie fallow for a season to restore the soil.
words.mnemonic: 'Fall + low' — activity falls low while the ground quietly rests.

words.definition: Unable to produce life or growth; barren; or completely free of germs.
words.example: Nothing would grow in the sterile, salt-poisoned ground near the old mine.
words.mnemonic: A 'steer' is a castrated bull that cannot breed — steer points to sterile.

words.definition: Extremely dry from heat or lack of water; or intensely thirsty.
words.example: By noon the parched riverbed had cracked into a maze of dusty plates.
words.mnemonic: Parched rhymes with 'scorched' — both are left bone-dry by the sun.

words.definition: To droop, sag, or lose freshness and strength, as a plant does.
words.example: The roses began to wilt within an hour of the vase running dry.
words.mnemonic: Wilt sounds like 'wither' — the flower's 'will' melts and it flops over.

words.definition: To grow gradually larger, stronger, or more complete over time.
words.example: As the moon began to wax, each night revealed a little more of its face.
words.mnemonic: Imagine dripping wax that builds up layer by layer, steadily growing bigger.

words.definition: To produce flowers, or to reach a healthy, vigorous, and flourishing state.
words.example: By late spring the orchard was in full bloom, every branch heavy with pink petals.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'room' — picture a room bursting open with fresh flowers.

words.definition: The act of making something fresh, valid, or active again after decline or expiry.
words.example: After the long winter, spring brought a sense of renewal to the tired, gray garden.
words.mnemonic: Break it up: re + new + al — to make something 'new' once more.

words.definition: A marked drop in performance, activity, or value, or a heavy sinking of the body.
words.example: Sales fell into a deep slump after the factory closed, and morale sank right along with them.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'slouch' plus 'dump' — you slouch and dump yourself into a chair.

words.definition: A temporary period when a country's economy shrinks and trade activity slows.
words.example: During the recession, hiring froze and shuttered storefronts lined the once-busy avenue.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'recedere,' to recede — imagine the economy receding like a retreating tide.

words.definition: Lacking physical strength, energy, or force; easily tired or overcome.
words.example: The old dog gave only a feeble wag of its tail before drifting back to sleep.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'flea' — as weak and easily crushed as a tiny flea.

words.definition: Having skin of an unhealthy yellowish or pale color.
words.example: After the long illness her once-rosy cheeks turned sallow and dull under the lamplight.
words.mnemonic: Swap the 'y' in 'yellow' for 's' — sallow is a sickly yellow tint.

words.definition: Growing thickly and abundantly; rich, dense, and profuse.
words.example: Vines and ferns grew so luxuriant that the path all but disappeared beneath them.
words.mnemonic: Hidden inside is 'luxury' — think of growth so lush it feels luxurious.

words.definition: A state of moral or cultural decline marked by excessive self-indulgence.
words.example: The empire's final years were steeped in decadence, its rulers feasting while the borders crumbled.
words.mnemonic: 'De-' (down) + 'cadence' (a fall, from Latin cadere) — a falling-down of morals.

words.definition: Shriveled and deeply wrinkled, especially from old age.
words.example: The wizened apple had sat in the bowl so long its skin puckered into deep creases.
words.mnemonic: Starts like 'wizard' — picture an ancient wizard with a shriveled, crinkled face.

words.definition: Twisted, knotty, and rough, as from age or hard wear.
words.example: The old sailor's gnarled hands gripped the rope, knuckles knotted like oak roots.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like a 'snarl' — a snarl of knots twisting through a tree's trunk.
